articles.title: At 11, Aneeshwar Kunchala is set to receive the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal for his wildlife-conservation work; he began campaigning against plastic pollution at four
articles.summary: Jane Goodall spent decades showing the world why protecting animals and their habitats matters to humanity.
articles.body: Jane Goodall spent decades showing the world why protecting animals and their habitats matters to humanity. Now, an 11-year-old conservationist is preparing to carry that message to a younger generation. Aneeshwar Kunchala, a UK-based wildlife presenter with family roots in Andhra Pradesh, India, is set to receive the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal for his work promoting wildlife conservation and biodiversity. According to The South Asia Times, Kunchala's journey began at just four, when he learnt about a whale that had died after ingesting plastic pollution. The experience inspired him to raise awareness about the threats facing wildlife.The medal was announced by STARMUS, an international festival bringing together science, space exploration, technology, music and the arts. In a statement issued on October 10, the festival named Aneeshwar as the recipient of the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal, recognising his efforts to encourage children to protect the natural world. The award is scheduled to be presented during STARMUS VIII, taking place in Tenerife and La Palma in Spain's Canary Islands from October 17 to 22, 2026.An incident that changed his perspectiveKunchala's interest in conservation began in his first year at school. In an interview with National Geographic Kids, he recalled how his teacher showed the class a picture of a whale that had died because of plastic pollution. He was shocked by the image and the fact that discarded plastic could kill such a large animal.The incident stayed with him and prompted him to think about what he could do to help wildlife. Although he was only four, the experience became the starting point for his efforts to educate others about protecting animals and the environment.In 2020, Kunchala began filming videos about animals with his father. Their first video focused on a baby robin in their garden, which he named Regee. The videos gave him an early platform to share his enthusiasm for wildlife and explain why animals and their habitats deserve protection. Over time, his activities expanded into television, documentary presenting, writing, poetry, art and public speaking.From wildlife videos to international audiencesOne of his major milestones came in 2022, when he presented COP27: Six Ways to Save Our Planet, a documentary addressing ways to tackle environmental challenges. Guinness World Records recognised him as the youngest male documentary presenter for the programme, at seven years and 288 days old.He has since appeared in wildlife and educational programming associated with broadcasters including the BBC, Sky Kids and Channel 5. His work has also included Go Wild with Steve Backshall, a CBeebies programme in which he learnt about animals, conservation and filmmaking alongside the naturalist and television presenter. He has described working with Backshall as one of the most memorable experiences of his career.His achievements extend beyond television. Guinness World Records lists three records associated with his work, including youngest male documentary presenter, youngest male newspaper columnist and the most animal sounds identified in one minute by an individual under 16. In January 2025, he identified 28 different animal sounds in a minute for the latter record. He has also written about endangered animals and used his own drawings and paintings to communicate his interest in nature.In 2024, Kunchala received the Diana Award for his work involving children and wildlife conservation. He has also been recognised through the British Citizen Youth Award and the Young Scientific Explorer honorary award from the Scientific Exploration Society. His other roles include serving as a National Trust ambassador and becoming the first young columnist for National Geographic Kids UK, where he contributes advice on helping wildlife, seasonal nature activities and citizen science projects.Following Jane Goodall's conservation legacyThe Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal connects Kunchala's work with the legacy of the renowned primatologist and conservationist, who devoted her life to studying chimpanzees and advocating for animal welfare and environmental protection. The medal recognises efforts to preserve biodiversity and encourage greater responsibility towards life on Earth.STARMUS established the Junior recognition to celebrate young people whose work reflects the importance of science, environmental stewardship and public engagement. The festival has also announced the Junior Stephen Hawking Medal for Spanish science communicator Valeria Corrales, highlighting two different ways in which young people can bring scientific and environmental ideas to wider audiences.Kunchaala's approach combines storytelling with practical encouragement, particularly for children who may feel too young to make a difference. In a February 2023 interview with Scouts UK, Kunchala summed up his conservation mission with the words, “Please save the animals and make sure the world looks beautiful.” It reflects the central idea behind his work: that caring about nature can begin with a single experience and grow into sustained efforts to educate others.When asked about his hope for the future, he told National Geographic Kids, "My dream is a future where wildlife is safe, valued and able to thrive alongside humans."You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2012, Barbra Streisand gave $10 million to support a Cedars-Sinai women's heart centre; 14 years later, it provides research-driven cardiac care to more than 1,700 women each year
articles.summary: In 2012, Barbra Streisand donated $10 million to Cedars-Sinai to create a research centre focused on women’s cardiovascular health.
articles.body: In 2012, Barbra Streisand donated $10 million to Cedars-Sinai to create a research centre focused on women’s cardiovascular health. The gift helped establish the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center, a facility dedicated to understanding why heart disease can affect women differently from men and improving diagnosis and treatment for female patients. According to Cedars-Sinai, the centre now provides research-driven cardiac care to more than 1,700 women each year.The donation was not simply a high-profile act of philanthropy. It responded to a long-standing gap in medicine, where heart disease research has often relied heavily on male subjects while women’s symptoms and underlying conditions can differ. Fourteen years on, the centre remains focused on closing that gap through patient care, research, and education.Why women’s heart health needed attentionHeart disease is the leading cause of death among women in the United States. Cedars-Sinai says more than 500,000 women die from cardiovascular disease each year, a figure greater than deaths from all cancers combined.Despite that scale, women have historically been underrepresented in heart-related studies. Streisand’s own website cites a Los Angeles Times report noting that women made up less than a quarter of participants in heart-related studies, while women’s heart disease was also less likely to be properly diagnosed than men’s.Cardiologist Bernadine Healy described the problem as “Yentl syndrome” in 1991, referencing the Streisand film about a woman who had to disguise herself as a man to receive an education. The idea was that women often received proper heart treatment only after showing symptoms that resembled those typically seen in men.Streisand’s $10 million giftStreisand’s $10 million contribution helped fund the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center at Cedars-Sinai. The donation was part of a broader campaign that raised more than $22 million for research into women’s cardiovascular health.The singer also helped recruit other major donors, including Michael Bloomberg, Barry Diller, Diane von Furstenberg, Ralph Lauren, Irwin Jacobs, Ronald Perelman, Sumner Redstone, and Haim Saban. Several contributed $1 million each, helping expand the centre’s research capacity.Streisand said she had long been angered by inequality, including gender discrimination in medicine. She argued that women deserved the same level of scientific attention and research investment as men, particularly in an area as serious as heart disease.How women’s heart disease can differOne of the centre’s central goals is to address the fact that heart disease does not always look the same in women and men. Cedars-Sinai explains that men more often experience the classic heart-attack symptom of chest pain during exertion, while women are more likely to report chest pressure, indigestion, shortness of breath, and fatigue.The underlying causes can differ as well. In men, heart disease is most commonly linked to a blocked coronary artery. In women, it is often caused by reduced blood flow in the heart’s small arteries, a condition known as microvascular coronary dysfunction.That difference matters because standard diagnostic tools may not reveal the problem in women. The centre says it is developing new treatment strategies and comprehensive risk assessments based on these biological differences.Research-driven care for womenThe Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center provides care to more than 1,700 women annually. Its work combines clinical treatment with research designed to improve how doctors identify and manage cardiovascular disease in female patients.Cedars-Sinai says the centre is one of only a few medical centres worldwide to use an adenosine cardiac magnetic resonance imaging stress test for diagnosing heart disease. The centre says this tool is better than an angiogram, the standard diagnostic approach for men, at revealing microvascular coronary dysfunction in women.The centre’s approach reflects a shift away from treating women’s heart disease as a smaller version of men’s disease. By studying sex-specific symptoms, risk factors, and diagnostic patterns, it aims to help doctors detect problems earlier and tailor treatment more effectively.A legacy of advocacyStreisand’s involvement went beyond writing a cheque. She worked with Dr Noel Bairey Merz, the centre’s medical director, to raise awareness and funding for women’s cardiovascular research. The two also delivered a TED Talk on the issue in the years before the centre’s dedication.Merz said women’s health research was often constrained by political debates and by the perception that heart disease was less urgent than other conditions. She hoped private philanthropy could help stabilise research funding and allow scientists to pursue questions that public grants did not always support.The centre’s work has helped bring greater attention to an issue that affects millions of women. Its focus on research, education, and clinical care reflects Streisand’s belief that women should not have to wait for their symptoms to resemble men’s before receiving appropriate treatment.Why the centre still mattersFourteen years after the donation, the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center continues to serve women whose symptoms may be overlooked or misunderstood. Its work remains important because cardiovascular disease continues to kill more women than all cancers combined.The centre also highlights the value of funding research that asks different questions. Instead of assuming that male-focused studies can fully explain women’s heart health, it examines how sex, symptoms, vascular function, and risk factors may interact in distinct ways.Streisand’s gift began as a response to a personal and societal concern, but its impact has endured. By helping create a centre dedicated to women’s hearts, she supported a model of care that treats women’s cardiovascular health as a priority in its own right.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Indiana man sketched a backyard pool on a napkin after a 1.5-year installation wait; two years later it became a 60,000-gallon private water park now renting for $140 an hour
articles.summary: Plenty of people dream about a backyard pool. Cory Johnson built a water park.
articles.body: Plenty of people dream about a backyard pool. Cory Johnson built a water park. On the east side of Lake Wawasee in Cromwell, his home shares its grounds with a 60,000-gallon private retreat that has waterfalls, a slide, a zip line and real palm tree trunks. Then he rents it out for $140 an hour!Walk in, and the first question is how anyone fitted a lagoon into a backyard. The second is obviously when you can book it!He wanted a pool, but they asked him to waitLike many others, Cory Johnson wanted a backyard pool where he could relax on the lounge chairs and enjoy his days. He initially set out to get a pool. A few years ago, he learned that the installation wait would stretch to about a year and a half, according to a report by inkfreenews. Rather than sitting around, he started sketching what he wanted on a napkin. That took him down memory lane.Ever since The Legend of Billie Jean came out, he had wanted a pool that he could jump into, or perhaps slide into straight from the house. "I watched the movie 'The Legend of Billie Jean' back in the '80s. (In) one of the scenes, a guy slides out of the window. He slides out of the window right into a pool. I said, 'I want to do that. I'm going to build that someday,'" he told Goshen News earlier.So, when he discovered that he would have to wait another year for the pool installation, he thought he would build it himself. "It can't be that hard," he told the outlet.Two pools in two yearsThe outdoor pool went up using blocks mortared together and reinforced with rebar. Johnson built the walls himself. Contractors poured the foundation, and Amish brothers finished much of the structure. The work took two years, including a six-month break in between. Both pools were finished in September 2023.The indoor pool took four days to fill! Cory Johnson's wife, Mandy, who was part of the project from the start, remembers checking the water line every morning. "Every morning, we'd wake up and come out here and see where the water line was. It was just neat every day to watch it fill up."The indoor/outdoor pool holds about 60,000 gallons of heated salt water, maintained at between 85 and 87 degrees year-round. Two pumps, two salt generators and oversized filters keep the water clean. Johnson still wants to cut back on chlorine, so he's thinking about adding a UV and ozone system.Inside the private backyard water parkThe indoor pool has a lagoon aesthetic. Fresh water rains down from a perforated pipe in a ceiling 20 to 30 feet up. A waterfall pours over giant rocks behind it. There is a zip line that sends guests flying towards them before they drop safely into the water.The custom slide is what catches people off guard. It ends higher above the water than most expect, so the ride is faster than they planned for. It sits on a 5-inch stainless steel pipe reinforced with concrete and rebar, then covered in stone so that it blends in. Mandy calls it a "beach vacation oasis".You can rent it for $140 an hourCory Johnson's pool in Cromwell won Swimply's Choice Award for 2026 for its distinctive design, which recreates the look of a waterfall landscape and incorporates natural outdoor elements into the pool area.Today, the Johnsons rent it out for $140 an hour. On average, they get five to six bookings a day. They also provide snorkelling gear, pool toys and professional underwater scooters used by scuba divers.The couple never planned to rent the pool. They hadn't even heard of Swimply when they started building. Now they rarely use the pool themselves, except for cleaning and maintenance.Mandy says many first-time guests don't believe the pool is real until they see it! One guest, who usually booked hotels or visited attractions for their daughter's birthday, said the experience at Johnson's property was the best yet. "This place is amazing! Every year for my daughter's birthday, we usually get a hotel so her friends and family can celebrate and swim. We have gone to Kalahari Yogi Bear camp ground ect. My daughter said this was the best birthday ever!" the review on Swimply reads. Another agreed: "The best space for a party! My son and his friends had an absolute blast. The host was also so laid back and pleasant to talk to. 10/10 would rent again and would recommend!"The pool stays open all year, so the Johnsons decorate it for winter with a 14-foot Christmas tree. Mandy says the children who walk in see the tree and the pool together, and it's "just like a double win for them".Cory Johnson isn't done. He's already dreaming about a steam cave and a hot spring that runs hotter than normal. "That'll probably never happen, but you never know. We don't like little. Go big or go home," he told the outlet.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand cabinet minister Rekha Arya’s husband, Girdhari Lal Sahu, released a video on Friday accusing her of corruption and alleging that she filed a police complaint against him on the basis of an AI-generated audio clip.In the video, Sahu questioned Arya’s decision to approach the police and demanded that she withdraw the allegations against him.“You have filed an FIR on the basis of an AI audio,” he said.Sahu also claimed that Arya was confident of remaining a minister for life and alleged that he had played a key role in her political rise.“The whole of Uttarakhand knows that I brought you to power,” he said, warning that she would not be forgiven by Baba Bankhandi Nath if she did not withdraw the allegations.“Wherever you are today is because of me,” he added.Sahu also accused Arya of corruption, alleging that she had amassed Rs 200 crore through corrupt practices. These allegations have not been independently verified.The video comes a day after Arya, a cabinet minister in the BJP government in Uttarakhand, filed an FIR against Sahu at Dehradun’s Cantt police station on October 15.She accused him of physical assault, harassment, caste-based abuse and death threats. The FIR includes provisions of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.In her complaint, Arya alleged that Sahu had concealed his previous marriage from her and that she later discovered he had a wife and children from an earlier relationship. She said she chose to remain silent at the time, following advice from family members and keeping their children’s future in mind.Arya further alleged that Sahu continued relationships with other women despite apologising to her, and that he subjected her to physical assault and verbal abuse when she objected.She also claimed to have obtained an audio recording in which Sahu was allegedly heard conspiring with a woman to kill her.After filing the complaint, Arya shared a video and the audio recording on social media, saying she had approached the police to protect her children. articles.title: As US universities vet CPT for international students; higher education groups seek court relief, hearing on November 6
articles.summary: A legal challenge to the Trump administration’s tighter interpretation of Curricular Practical Training (CPT) rules for international students is set to
articles.body: A legal challenge to the Trump administration’s tighter interpretation of Curricular Practical Training (CPT) rules for international students is set to come up for a hearing on Nov 6, with four major higher education organisations seeking to block the changes that have prompted several US universities to suspend or restrict CPT authorisations.The Association of American Universities (AAU), the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM) filed the lawsuit on Oct 5 in the US District Court (Massachusetts). They are seeking a preliminary injunction and a stay of agency action to pause the disputed interpretation while the case proceeds.“America’s colleges and universities have long attracted the world’s best talent not only because of the high-quality education and research that they offer, but also because of the practical learning opportunities US institutions offer for students’ future professional lives – including programs like CPT,” Barbara R. Snyder, president at AAU said.“Suddenly upending CPT just as the fall semester begins will have long-term negative consequences not only for our students and universities, but for all Americans,” she added.The Presidents’ Alliance said the changes had already disrupted students’ plans with colleges and universities across the country having paused or halted CPT authorizations, and students have already lost internships and other placements.The lawsuit challenges two broadcast messages issued by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), on Aug 12 and Aug 24, 2026. The messages set out a stricter interpretation of existing CPT requirements and highlighted the compliance responsibilities of designated school officials who authorise CPT for F-1 international students.CPT allows eligible F-1 students to undertake practical training directly related to their academic programmes. Under the revised federal interpretation, the training must be an integral part of an established curriculum and required of all students in the relevant degree programme for degree completion. An internship that carries academic credit but is optional may therefore no longer qualify.The organisations argue that the Trump administration has effectively changed how the existing regulations are applied through administrative messages, without following the formal rulemaking process. They contend that the move has created uncertainty for universities and students who had relied on established practices to arrange internships, practicums and other forms of experiential learning.NAFSA executive director and CEO Fanta Aw said the changes had placed university officials responsible for international student compliance in a difficult position. She said the abrupt changes had created “significant new restrictions and uncertainty” for designated school officials, who must advise international students and ensure that their institutions comply with immigration rules.The plaintiffs have asked the court to intervene and grant a preliminary injunction while the case is pending, arguing that the revised interpretation threatens students’ access to practical learning opportunities and creates compliance risks for institutions without adequate notice.Universities across the US have reviewed their CPT policies in response to the revised federal interpretation. The extent of the restrictions varies by institution and programme, with some universities pausing particular categories of CPT while continuing to process applications that meet the revised requirements.At Harvard University, several schools have stopped authorising CPT for placements that do not meet the revised criteria. It appears that CPT is currently unavailable for affected placements at Harvard Law School, Harvard Medical School, the Graduate School of Design and the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.Harvard’s international office says it will authorise CPT for F-1 students only when the opportunity is a formal requirement of the degree programme, successful completion of the degree is contingent on the training, and the required internship or practicum is offered by sponsoring employers through cooperative agreements with the school.The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) has temporarily paused new and pending CPT authorisation requests received or pending as of Aug 24, 2026, for training that is not required of all students in a degree programme.The University of Pennsylvania, meanwhile, has resumed processing CPT requests where the practical training is an integral and required component of the student’s established curriculum. “This resumption applies only to requests that meet the current federal requirements,” the university states.Berkeley has suspended applications for “Course Credit CPT”, but continues to process applications for degree programmes where an internship or field placement is a documented graduation requirement for all students. Yale University has also said it will process CPT requests when the training is integral to an established curriculum and required of all students in the programme for degree completion.According to immigration attorneys the Nov 6 hearing is expected to consider the plaintiffs’ requests for a preliminary injunction and a stay of agency action. If the court grants interim relief, it could temporarily block or limit enforcement of the challenged interpretation, depending on the terms of its order.You use AI every day. articles.summary: At an age when many people prefer to keep their feet firmly on the ground, Helga Duffy strapped herself to the wing of a plane and took to the skies.
articles.body: At an age when many people prefer to keep their feet firmly on the ground, Helga Duffy strapped herself to the wing of a plane and took to the skies. The 99-year-old set a Guinness World Records title for the oldest female wing-walker after completing the daring flight at RFC Rendcomb Airfield in Cirencester, Gloucestershire, on October 16, 2026. Inspired by another woman who performed the same stunt at 97, Duffy decided to pursue the extraordinary challenge herself. But her achievement was about more than breaking a record. articles.title: In the 1950s and 1960s, Western agencies seeded crested wheatgrass for grazing; by 1970s, it had altered 6.4 million acres of sagebrush, many never recovered
articles.summary: Discover how the introduction of crested wheatgrass in the 1950s and 60s has altered over 6.4 million acres of sagebrush ecosystems, affecting wildlife habitats and complicating restoration efforts.
articles.body: During the 1950s and 1960s, land management agencies across the western United States carried out extensive programmes with the aim of reducing sagebrush cover and establishing grasslands that could provide forage for livestock. Crested wheatgrass, a perennial grass introduced from Eurasia, was one of the principal plants used for this programme. This plant species established relatively easily and tolerated aggressive grazing.According to the US Forest Service, seeding with non-native grasses, primarily crested wheatgrass, had affected around 6.4 million acres of sagebrush land by the 1970s.This programme’s legacy continues to impact vegetation across the American West, with the agency reporting that many affected sites have not yet recovered their past ecological characteristics. Though it is important to note that the figure does not mean that all 6.4 million acres were converted in the same way or have remained unrecovered.Why agencies opted to plant crested wheatgrassSagebrush steppe ecosystems cover vast parts of the western United States, especially the Intermountain region. These landscapes contain a mixture of shrubs, native grasses and wildflowers and provide habitat for wildlife, including greater sage-grouse and pygmy rabbits. Livestock grazing, drought, and other forms of disturbances that occurred in the late 19th century through the early 20th century diminished native herbaceous plants across many landscapes. Several attempts were made to stabilise these degraded soils, maximise livestock forage, and maintain basic vegetative cover under what was then termed agricultural restoration. The US Forest Service suggested that overgrazing was not solely responsible for all the transformations occurring in sagebrush lands.Crested wheatgrass turned into a favoured option because it was relatively easy to establish, tolerated grazing and could produce substantial forage. Researchers James A. Young and Raymond A. Evans documented its growing use in the Intermountain region during the decades following its introduction. After World War II, advances in both methods and machinery for sowing crested wheatgrass led to its widespread use on range restoration sites. Seeding also helped control other plants and improve grazing conditions.Millions of acres experienced lasting changesSince the 1930s, methods such as prescribed burns, herbicides, mechanical treatment, and grass seeding have been used in order to reduce the area covered by sagebrush. Such actions were most intensive in the 1950s and 1960s, and the goal was usually to convert brush land into grassland that would be appropriate for livestock grazing. The US Forest Service claims that grass seeding, mainly non-native species, especially crested wheatgrass, affected about 6.4 million acres of sagebrush land by the 1970s. Such statistics relate to the land affected by grass seeding but not converted into one kind of grass.Crested wheatgrass can establish itself in dense colonies and thereby become a competitor to other plants and inhibit the development of native grass and flowers. Once established, it dominates native vegetation and actively arrests the return of local flora, especially in places where sagebrush seeds are unavailable.The consequences extend beyond changes in plant composition. Sagebrush provides food and shelter for wildlife adapted to shrubland habitats, while a grass-dominated site can offer a different structure and range of resources. For example, greater sage-grouse depend on shrublands for parts of their lifecycle. Thus, when shrublands are replaced by extensive grasses, this can lead to a loss of suitable habitat in some areas. The extent of the effect will vary depending on the area affected and the habitat needs of the species involved.Why recovery remains challengingRestoring native vegetation in established crested wheatgrass stands can be challenging because the grass competes with newly introduced plants. A 2021 study published in Restoration Ecology tested chemical and mechanical treatments intended to suppress crested wheatgrass before native species were seeded. The authors of the paper state that these approaches failed to provide better establishment of the natives. At the end of the experiment, the density of seedlings was almost the same for all the treatments, suggesting that suppression of the grass was not enough to ensure successful restoration.However, minimal recovery occurs only under highly specific environmental constraints. According to the U.S. Forest Service, sagebrush occasionally establishes sparse footholds within ageing stands of crested wheatgrass, though these isolated instances do not equate to a systemic return of the native steppe. Results of restoration efforts will depend on things like seed availability, climate, grazing, and the techniques used to prepare the site. The application of crested wheatgrass has become one of the last resorts in the contemporary approach to erosion control, where soil stabilisation is given priority or where invasion by non-native grasses is being prevented.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2016, a Florida diver reported possible human remains offshore, leading archaeologists to uncover a 7,200-year-old Native American burial site now submerged underwater
articles.summary: A 7,200-year-old Native American burial site was uncovered off Manasota Key, Florida, after an amateur diver reported possible human remains, revealing significant archaeological findings about Florida’s Indigenous past.
articles.body: In June 2016, an amateur diver searching for prehistoric fossils off Manasota Key, which is located in Florida, reported possible human remains to the state’s Bureau of Archaeological Research. The investigation that followed the report revealed a prehistoric Native American burial site beneath the Gulf of Mexico. Known as the Manasota Key Offshore (MKO) archaeological site, it contains human remains. Additionally, the site contains worked wooden stakes that were linked to ancient burial practices. According to the Florida Department of State, radiocarbon dating of two wooden stakes placed them at more than 7,200 years old, thus transforming the site into an important source of evidence about Florida’s Indigenous past and the region’s changing landscape.How a fossil hunter’s report led to an archaeological investigationPrompted by the fossil hunter's initial report, underwater archaeologists from the state’s Bureau of Archaeological Research launched an investigation of the region using non-invasive techniques. The methods included magnetometry, side-scan sonar and sub-bottom profiling. These helped the researchers map features beneath the water and identify areas for further examination. Several areas containing peat, worked wooden stakes and the remains of multiple individuals were documented in the investigation. After the initial investigation had established that the offshore location contained a prehistoric burial site, on February 28, 2018, the discovery was announced publicly by Florida’s secretary of state.Following these initial non-invasive tracking surveys, the methodology transitioned to targeted, physical salvage operations. In the excavations conducted between 2017 and 2018, the crew recovered human remains representing at least 11 individuals. A federal notice published by the National Park Service documented seven adults, two infants and two unborn individuals, along with 49 associated funerary objects. Fibre cordage, wooden stakes and modified shells were recovered from the site. Therefore, the notice established the minimum number of individuals represented by the recovered items instead of necessarily establishing the total number of people originally buried across the entire site.How a prehistoric burial site became submergedThe burial site was likely not underwater when it was in use. Researchers believe it occupied a freshwater pond with a peat-rich bottom, located on land before rising sea levels inundated the site. The state’s agency reported that the Gulf of Mexico’s water level was approximately 30 feet lower than it is today. The site currently lies beneath about 21 feet of water. Because the sea level in the Gulf of Mexico was roughly 30 feet lower than today when the site was in use 7,200 years ago, the former freshwater pond was situated on dry land roughly nine feet above the sea level of that era. With the rise in sea level, the pond became a part of the submerged landscape beneath the Gulf.The peat underneath the pond helped preserve evidence of the burial site. In its 2018 announcement, the state’s department explained that peat slows organic decay and that the pond’s peat bottom remained as it was even after rising seas covered the area. The survival of the materials found alongside the human remains allowed archaeologists to study evidence that might otherwise have deteriorated.The wooden stakes hold special importance because radiocarbon dating of two examples provided evidence of the site’s antiquity. The Florida Department of State dates the stakes to more than 7,200 years ago, during the Archaic Period.Why the discovery matters for archaeologyFlorida’s archaeological record already includes Archaic-period pond burials at sites like Windover in Titusville and Little Salt Spring in Sarasota County. The distinguishing point for Manasota Key is its offshore location and the preservation of a prehistoric burial environment beneath the Gulf of Mexico. The site offers researchers an opportunity to reconstruct a landscape that existed before sea-level rise submerged it. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that continental shelves and other submerged coastal areas preserve evidence of communities that lived there thousands of years ago.The discovery also raises questions about the protection and respectful treatment of human remains. A federal notice records that the state’s agency consulted representatives of the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians, the Seminole Tribe of Florida and the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma when assessing the recovered remains and associated funerary objects. The notice states that the remains were determined to be Native American based on contextual data and osteological analysis.The MKO is protected under Florida Law. The state’s Division of Historical Resources says unauthorised excavation or removal of archaeological material is prohibited, while knowingly destroying or damaging a human burial can constitute a felony under state law. Officials have emphasised the need to protect the site from intentional and accidental disturbance by divers and other visitors. Therefore, its management combines archaeological investigation with the safeguarding of a culturally important burial ground.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2026, a Florida man went lobster diving and spotted a torpedo-shaped object; the Navy later detonated a suspected WWII-era munition
articles.summary: In August 2026, diver Luke Neiman spotted a torpedo-shaped object while lobster diving near Fort Pierce, Florida. The Navy later confirmed it as a suspected WWII-era munition and conducted a controlled detonation.
articles.body: Fort Pierce sits on Florida’s Atlantic coast in St. Lucie County, on a stretch known as the Treasure Coast. Its inlet and nearby reef ledges draw recreational divers who hunt lobster. The area was a United States Navy amphibious training site during World War II, and divers there have reported finding old ordnance before. In August 2026, diver Luke Neiman went lobster diving with his father and a friend off Florida’s coast, and CubaHeadlines, citing WESH 2 News, reported that he found an object he believed was a torpedo. They were working south of the Fort Pierce jetty, an area Neiman visits often for lobster. He reported the object to Florida wildlife officers, and CubaHeadlines reported that the Navy later destroyed it in an underwater detonation. The Navy described it as a suspected munition from World War II.Luke Neiman’s August dive south of the Fort Pierce jettyCubaHeadlines reported that the commission informed the US Coast Guard, the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office bomb squad and the Navy. Neiman saw something that did not quite fit into the reef. As CubaHeadlines described it, Neiman inspected the object and noticed an end and a cone, which led him to think it might be a torpedo. He returned to the boat, marked the exact location with his father, and informed the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission about the discovery.The September 15, 2026 Navy disposal off St. Lucie CountyCubaHeadlines reported that the commission informed the US Coast Guard, the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office bomb squad and the Navy. Navy explosive ordnance disposal personnel then carried out an underwater detonation on September 15, 2026, which the Navy’s statement called a routine underwater munition disposal operation. That wording describes the Navy’s operation, not the discovery itself. The statement identified the object as a suspected World War II-era munition. The statements cited here give no type, model, or origin for the object.The Department of Defense’s November 2016 report on munitions disposed at seaThere is a technical explanation for the warning. The Department of Defense’s November 2016 report to Congress, Research Related to Effect of Ocean Disposal of Munitions in U.S. Coastal Waters, examines the challenges of assessing and managing munitions disposed of at sea. The department’s Ordnance Reef pages say that sea disposal of unserviceable munitions was an accepted practice until the 1970s, so the location and condition of such munitions are often uncertain. That uncertainty is why the department advises people to use its “Recognize, Retreat, Report” safety program instead of trying to retrieve a suspected munition themselves: recognize that it is dangerous, retreat without approaching, touching, moving, or disturbing it, and report it by calling 911. Whether Neiman’s object was a result of disposal or training is not mentioned anywhere in public sources.The Fort Pierce training base that closed in 1946The area has a documented military past. The National Navy UDT-SEAL Museum states that the Naval Amphibious Training Base at Fort Pierce closed in 1946 after about 140,000 men had received some form of training there. The museum’s own pages give both June 1943 and July 1943 for the start of the first Naval Combat Demolition Unit class, while the Navy’s All Hands magazine says the NCDU training school was established at Fort Pierce on June 6, 1943. The Museum of Florida History adds that trainees also learned to operate various landing craft.DIVE Magazine reported that discoveries of historical military ordnance are not uncommon along Florida’s Treasure Coast, where the US military conducted amphibious warfare training before the Normandy invasion during World War II. Diver Tom Gramlich’s find of a World War II-era device near Pepper Park in Fort Pierce, which the METIS event log dates to January 13, 2026.What a NOAA survey of a Hawaii munitions site foundThe appendix of the above-mentioned study summarises the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s 2007 Ordnance Reef Survey Project Report. According to the FAQ, the military had done a survey of this area in 2002 in which they had found more than 2,000 military ordnance, all of which were under 60 feet in depth, that are unfuzed, unfired, and not chemical in nature. The study conducted by NOAA will use seafloor imaging technology, a remotely operated vehicle, and independent testing of fish, sediments, and water.The report concluded that the effects of sea-disposed munitions in US coastal waters appear to be minimal, and that removing them would do more harm to marine life and the ocean environment than leaving them in place. It based these conclusions on research at two Hawaii sites. They also state that the department will dispatch explosive ordnance disposal staff if there is a threat to public safety from the munitions. The report’s general advice to leave disposal-site munitions in place therefore does not explain the Navy’s decision to detonate the object, because the sources consulted do not say it came from a disposal site.You use AI every day. articles.title: Japan issued alert for 'largest recorded' 9.9 magnitude earthquake, but ground didn't shake: What happened
articles.summary: Japan triggered widespread alarm on Friday after its earthquake early warning system \"announced\" a magnitude-9.9 earthquake alert, prompting emergency
articles.body: Japan triggered widespread alarm on Friday after its earthquake early warning system "announced" a magnitude-9.9 earthquake alert, prompting emergency phone alerts, public loudspeaker warnings and television broadcasts urging people to take shelter, before the warning was withdrawn eight minutes later.However, no major shaking followed the alert, which the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) later attributed to errors in its earthquake magnitude estimation and location calculations. The agency is investigating the cause of the malfunction, reportd Japan Times.The alert was issued at 12.40 pm (local time), two minutes after a magnitude-6.9 earthquake struck off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The warning incorrectly placed the epicentre near the Kuril Islands and predicted seismic intensity of up to shindo 7, the highest level on Japan's seven-point seismic intensity scale, across areas stretching from Hokkaido to the Tokai region.In Japan, however, the recorded shaking reached only shindo 1, a level at which vibrations may be barely noticeable. At 12.48 pm (local time), the JMA issued a cancellation notice, marking the first time an emergency earthquake warning had been formally withdrawn, according to the agency.The predicted magnitude of 9.9 also drew attention because it exceeded the magnitude of any earthquake recorded in history. The 1960 earthquake off Chile's Biobio region, the strongest on record, measured magnitude 9.5. The JMA said 9.9 was the highest magnitude its system could communicate externally.Ayataka Ebita, head of the JMA's earthquake and tsunami observation division, said the system had mistakenly estimated the earthquake's epicentre and overstated its magnitude. The agency ruled out a cyberattack and said it was examining how the error occurred.At a subsequent briefing, the JMA said the system had applied a magnitude formula designed for earthquakes within Japan to a quake occurring far away. It had also used different estimated locations to calculate the magnitude and forecast shaking, although both calculations should have been based on the same location.The investigation is continuing. Ebita said lightning was not believed to have caused the error, adding that the processing of seismic sensor data could have contributed to the malfunction.In Tokyo on Friday, pedestrians paused to check their phones as warnings circulated, while users of the NERV Disaster Prevention app received a magnitude-9.9 alert accompanied by a countdown to shaking that never materialised.Lola Milroy-Tompkins, a 20-year-old British student at Waseda University in Tokyo, said she was eating lunch in a campus cafeteria when the alarm sounded.“I have never experienced an earthquake before and I expected the grand style shaking and everything to start falling around me,” she said.She recalled students worrying and talking among themselves as they tried to understand what was happening, but the anticipated earthquake never arrived.The JMA's early warning system automatically combines readings from seismometers at observation stations to estimate an earthquake's location, magnitude and expected intensity. Ebita said the reliability of such estimates depends on the number of observation stations and the quality of their readings, which can deteriorate when an earthquake occurs far from monitoring equipment.The incident also disrupted public transport. The Tokaido Shinkansen line was halted for 15 minutes after an automated safety system was triggered, Central Japan Railway said. Government officials reported no damage related to the Kamchatka earthquake.Chief cabinet secretary Minoru Kihara said the government took seriously the anxiety caused by the warning and the burden on people who evacuated or took precautionary measures, as well as those whose travel and business activities were disrupted.False alarms have occurred previously. In July 2020, the JMA issued a warning covering 15 prefectures, including Tokyo, after incorrectly estimating an earthquake's location and magnitude. In August 2013, noise from a seabed seismometer was mistakenly combined with readings from a small earthquake, triggering widespread warnings across the Kinki region. Neither incident produced shaking of shindo 1 or higher, according to the JMA.The agency's website noted that false alarms can result from sensor noise caused by accidents, lightning or equipment failures.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A new housing development in Los Angeles will provide 97 permanent apartments to women and survivors of violence who have experienced homelessness, with
articles.body: A new housing development in Los Angeles will provide 97 permanent apartments to women and survivors of violence who have experienced homelessness, with American singer Miley Cyrus' foundation contributing $1 million towards the project. The apartments are being built at Rosa's Place in the city's Skid Row neighbourhood by the Downtown Women's Center (DWC), which expects the development to open in 2027.The contribution was announced on October 10 at a fundraising event organised by DWC, Imprintent reported. During the event, the organisation also honoured Cyrus and her mother, Tish Cyrus-Purcell, for their involvement in its housing programmes. The event raised $3.2 million, including the amount pledged by the Miley Cyrus Foundation.The new apartments will form part of DWC's existing campus in downtown Los Angeles. According to its official website, the organisation has spent nearly five decades working with women and survivors of violence, providing accommodation and services intended to help them achieve greater stability. Rosa's Place is the latest addition to that work.Cyrus and her mother have also visited the centre, met women receiving assistance and helped with improvements to residential and shared spaces. Their involvement extends to discussions about the interior design of the new building.A closer look at Rosa's PlaceRosa's Place is one of the projects being funded through DWC's HOME Campaign, an initiative focused on increasing housing and services at its downtown campus.The development is intended to provide more than just residential accommodation. Alongside the 97 apartments, DWC plans to establish a service hub within the building, allowing residents to receive additional assistance as they work towards maintaining stable housing.An important part of the project is its trauma-informed approach which takes into account the experiences of women and survivors who may have faced violence or homelessness. DWC says the housing and support facilities are being developed around the needs of the people who will use them.Miley Cyrus and her mother's role Miley and Tish have contributed ideas for renovations at the downtown campus. Their involvement has also included meeting women who use DWC's services. "One of the most meaningful parts of our partnership has been meeting the women at DWC and hearing their stories. Their strength, resilience, and hope stay with me long after I leave," Cyrus said as quoted by ImprintentTish has also spoken about the importance she places on the surroundings in which women receive assistance. "I’ve always believed that home is our safe place and can have a powerful impact on how we feel. Helping design spaces at DWC where women can rest, heal, and look toward the future means so much to me," she said.Raising $3.2 million The announcement formed part of the 2026 Every Woman Housed Gala, an annual fundraising event organised by DWC. This year's gathering took place under the theme It All Starts at Home and was hosted by actor, writer and producer Natasha Rothwell.Nearly 600 people attended, including community leaders, advocates, corporate representatives and other supporters of the organisation.Before the foundation's contribution was announced, the event had generated $2.2 million through donations, sponsorships and ticket sales. articles.title: UAE visa fraud alert: Indian embassy warns nationals against agencies promising jobs, residency
articles.summary: Indian nationals in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have been warned against fraudulent visa and migration agencies allegedly collecting fees for overseas
articles.body: Indian nationals in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have been warned against fraudulent visa and migration agencies allegedly collecting fees for overseas employment and residency services without delivering on their promises or refunding applicants.In an advisory dated October 12, the Embassy of India in Abu Dhabi and the Consulate General of India in Dubai and the Northern Emirates said they had received complaints against agencies advertising third-country employment and residency visa services through social media.According to Khaleej Times, the missions cautioned Indians against relying solely on online advertisements or trusting private visa processing agencies, particularly those operating outside India. Such agencies allegedly collect money from applicants but fail to provide the promised services or return the fees.Verify visa details through official channelsThe missions urged Indian nationals seeking employment or residency opportunities abroad to check the credibility of visa processing agencies before making payments.Applicants were advised to verify visa requirements, application procedures and authorised channels directly with the embassy or consulate of the destination country in their country of residence. They were also asked to consult official government and embassy websites for accurate and updated information.The advisory stressed that no private agency can guarantee visa approval, as the final decision rests solely with the government issuing the visa.“Never pay any amount based on promises of visa approval,” the missions said, according to Khaleej Times, warning applicants against placing blind trust in private visa processing intermediaries.Earlier warning flagged misuse of personal dataThe latest advisory follows an August 24 warning by the Indian Embassy in Abu Dhabi against unauthorised individuals offering assistance with visa regularisation, emergency certificates, exit permits, Emirates IDs and employment-related procedures.The earlier advisory cautioned that personal documents and biometric information shared with unauthorised individuals could be misused to obtain bank accounts, loans and credit cards without the victims’ knowledge.Indian nationals were advised not to share passport details, Emirates ID information or biometric data with unauthorised persons. Biometric information required for official procedures should be provided only at authorised UAE government facilities.The embassy also directed Indians seeking assistance to the Pravasi Bharatiya Sahayata Kendra.The missions have urged Indian nationals in the UAE to verify immigration-related claims through official channels and exercise caution before paying agents or sharing sensitive personal information.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the late 1800s, homesteaders planted smooth brome in what is now Grand Teton National Park for cattle feed; a restoration effort targeting 4,500 acres began in 2007
articles.summary: Grand Teton National Park is actively restoring historic hayfields to native sagebrush-steppe habitats, enhancing wildlife populations and biodiversity. Learn about their ongoing efforts and the impact on ecosystems.
articles.body: In the late 1800s, in what is now Grand Teton National Park, homesteaders converted native sagebrush grasslands into hayfields to feed their livestock year-round. A non-native perennial grass called the smooth brome was planted; it grew in the region’s short, cool seasons. Eventually, the agricultural field covered roughly 4,500 acres and became known as the Kelly Hayfields.Cultivation gradually faded when Grand Teton National Park expanded in 1950 to include Mormon Row. The National Park Service acquired more land during the 1960s, but pasture grasses persisted. The non-native vegetation continued to grow without irrigation but yielded less seasonal food compared to native sagebrush-grassland communities after the growing season had passed. In 2007, the National Park Service ratified a long-term effort to restore approximately 4,500 acres of former hayfields to native sagebrush-steppe habitat. The programme’s objective was to reestablish plant communities that provided food and shelter for wildlife. In June 2021, the Park staff expanded their restoration effort onto another 110 acres across two southern zones of the Park.How Grand Teton is restoring former hayfieldsThe 2021 project spanned 90 acres within the South Slough unit, located west of Mormon Row, alongside 20 acres in the McBride unit, situated south of Jackson Hole Airport. The South Slough project contributes to the Antelope Flats sagebrush restoration outlined in the Park’s 2007 Elk and Bison Management Plan, whereas the McBride project is solely focused on restoring sage grouse habitat.The process involves removing the non-native pasture grass as Park staff utilise herbicide through tractors, utility terrain vehicles, and backpack sprayers. The treatment eradicates the existing vegetation, leaving the ground bare, and once the grass is removed, the area is seeded with a mixture of native grasses, shrubs, and forbs, or flowering herbaceous plants.Restoration requires more than just clearing a field, and the absence of an effective strategy prompted Park biologists to analyse possible methods. During the 1990s, they carried out a series of small, controlled experiments to replace the persistent pasture grasses, and plans were formalised in 2007 with the Grand Teton National Park Foundation’s support. As per the National Park Service, reports indicate 1,320 acres were in various stages of restoration in 2021, with advanced sites supporting sagebrush, wildflowers, and established native plants.Restored landscapes show signs of wildlife useAccording to the National Park Service, sage grouse changed their behaviour from avoiding the former hayfields to utilising the restored landscape, while Park field observations confirmed elk, bison, and pronghorn followed suit.Moreover, the return of native flowering plants and the establishment of more diverse plant communities were particularly important because these sagebrush-steppe ecosystems provide essential food and habitat for native species year-round. However, the accounts do not quantify increases in wildlife populations, so observations show use of the area, not a specific rise in animal numbers.As part of a larger conservation effort in the landscape, the Kelly Hayfields project leverages its strategic location between the Snake River and the Gros Ventre Mountains. It does so by connecting newly restored habitats directly to existing sagebrush-steppe zones like those protected in Antelope Flats. The foundation’s other project includes restoration at Kelly Warm Springs and Ditch Creek, aligned with initiatives to stabilise and enhance the Mormon Row Historic District. To facilitate this project, the Grand Teton National Park Foundation contributed more than $120,000 to the Kelly Hayfields project, backed by private donors, the Teton Conservation District, and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Snoop Dogg's Dr. Bombay has moved from a digital ape character to a $249 collectible figure, while a rare Homies prototype is being offered for $15,000
articles.summary: Snoop Dogg’s digital ape character, Dr.
articles.body: Snoop Dogg’s digital ape character, Dr. Bombay, has taken another step into the world of physical collectibles, with a limited-edition figure priced at $249.99 making its debut at New York Comic Con in October 2026. At the same time, Vital Toys is offering a rare Homies P-Rico production sample for $15,000, bringing an unusual piece of toy-making history out of its archives. The two releases connect the growing market for digital-inspired merchandise with the nostalgia surrounding hip-hop collectibles from the early 2000s.How did Snoop Dogg’s Dr. Bombay become a $249 collectible figureAccording to EIN Presswire, on behalf of Vital Toys, the company introduced its Dr. Bombay collectible at New York Comic Con, with the figure available exclusively through Walmart website. The launch brings a character associated with digital art into the physical toy market, allowing collectors to own a tangible version of the ape.Dr. Bombay is inspired by Bored Ape Yacht Club NFT number 6723, which belongs to rapper Snoop Dogg. The character's transition into a physical product reflects an effort to connect online collectibles with a broader audience beyond people familiar with digital assets.The figure stands 13 inches tall and reproduces several distinctive elements associated with the character. Its outfit includes a pink coat, camouflage trousers, a helmet and combat boots. The design also incorporates the bold accessories and streetwear-inspired appearance that distinguish Dr. Bombay from conventional toy figures.Vital Toys has priced the collectible at $249.99. Rather than simply reproducing the digital image, the company has developed a full-sized character with a detailed outfit, presenting it as a display piece for collectors.A collaboration rooted in early hip-hop toy cultureThe partnership between Snoop Dogg and Vital Toys predates the Dr. Bombay release by more than two decades. According to The Bored Ape Gazette, the company previously worked with the rapper in the early 2000s to develop 6 action figures inspired by him.One of those figures appeared in the music video for his song From Tha Church To Da Palace, connecting the toys directly with his music career. The collaboration brought the rapper's recognisable image into a format that fans could collect and display.Vital Toys founder and chief executive Sidney Richlin is central to both the earlier projects and the latest release. His experience in producing entertainment-related merchandise has helped bring Dr. Bombay from a digital character into a physical collectible.The Bored Ape Gazette reported that Richlin and Snoop Dogg renewed their collaboration in 2023, using the rapper's Bored Ape character as the basis for the new figure.Richlin has also described the project as an opportunity to demonstrate how intellectual property associated with Bored Ape Yacht Club can reach mainstream retail.What makes the rare Homies P-Rico prototype worth $15,000Alongside Dr. Bombay, Vital Toys is offering a collectible with a different kind of appeal. According to EIN Presswire, the item is an original Homies P-Rico production sample made in 2004 and preserved in the company's archives for more than 20 years.The approximately 7.5-inch figure belongs to Series 2 of the Homies collection. It features a custom necklace, a microphone, a New York jersey and a headwrap displaying the Puerto Rican flag.Its asking price is $15,000, considerably higher than the price of the Dr. Bombay figure. The difference reflects the P-Rico sample's claimed rarity and historical background rather than its size alone.Vital Toys says only 2 original samples were produced. One remained with Richlin, while the other was given to Homies creator David Gonzales and was subsequently destroyed. Richlin's example is now described by the company as the only known surviving version.The sample's long period in the company's archives adds another layer to its story. Unlike a standard retail figure manufactured in larger quantities, this piece represents an early production stage and preserves a connection to the process through which the Homies toy was developed.The company is offering the item through Walmart website during the New York Comic Con event, giving collectors an opportunity to acquire an object that has not been part of an ordinary retail release.New York Comic Con brings two generations of collectibles togetherThe October launch also provides a platform for Richlin to revisit the company's history. According to EIN Presswire, he was scheduled to appear in a livestream from the Walmart booth at New York Comic Con on October 10 at 11 am Eastern time, discussing the collectibles and sharing stories from his career.The Bored Ape Gazette reported that Richlin sees the Dr. Bombay project as a potential route for other Bored Ape Yacht Club members to bring their characters into mainstream retail. The approach treats a digital character as commercial intellectual property that can be developed into products for audiences who may not participate in NFT markets.Founded in 1998, Vital Toys has worked on collectibles inspired by music, films, art and popular culture.You use AI every day. articles.title: Michael Jackson's original red-and-black 'Thriller' jacket and the glove he wore during his moonwalk debut are returning to auction, with the glove estimated at up to $800,000
articles.summary: Michael Jackson’s original red-and-black leather jacket from the Thriller music video and the rhinestone-covered glove he wore during his first televised
articles.body: Michael Jackson’s original red-and-black leather jacket from the Thriller music video and the rhinestone-covered glove he wore during his first televised moonwalk are returning to auction in December 2026. The two iconic pieces of entertainment history will be offered by Julien’s Auctions as part of its upcoming Celebrity & Pop Culture Experience in Abu Dhabi. The glove carries an estimated value of $600,000 to $800,000, while the jacket could potentially exceed $10 million. Both items previously achieved record-breaking sales, adding to the anticipation surrounding their return.Michael Jackson’s Thriller jacket and moonwalk glove returning to auctionAccording to Julien’s Auctions, the original Thriller jacket and the glove worn during Jackson’s performance at Motown 25 are among 4 significant items from his career being offered in December. The sale will also feature the black leather loafers he wore in the Thriller music video and the shoes associated with his televised moonwalk debut.The auction house announced the upcoming sale on 7 October 2026, describing the collection as a group of objects that helped shape music, fashion and popular culture. The items are returning to the auction market after nearly two decades, giving collectors another opportunity to acquire pieces associated with defining moments in Jackson’s career.The Michael Jackson: The Fashion Legacy evening auction is scheduled for 7 December at the Rosewood Abu Dhabi. A further day auction will take place on 8 December, forming part of the wider 3-day Celebrity & Pop Culture Experience.How the rhinestone glove became a piece of music historyThe glove is closely associated with Jackson’s performance of Billie Jean during the 1983 television special Motown 25: Yesterday, Today, Forever. During the performance, he introduced the moonwalk to a worldwide television audience, creating one of the most memorable moments in modern pop music.The single white glove, decorated with sparkling rhinestones, became an instantly recognisable part of his stage appearance. Its connection to the performance has given it significance beyond its physical design, linking it to a moment that helped establish Jackson as a global entertainment icon.Africanews reported that Julien’s Auctions expects the glove to fetch between $600,000 and $800,000. Executive director Martin Nolan explained that the estimate reflects the item's previous sale and the potential competition among international bidders.The glove was last sold at Julien’s Auctions in November 2009, when Hong Kong businessman Hoffman Ma acquired it for a reported $430,000. The auction house has also cited a figure of $420,000 before the buyer’s premium when discussing the earlier transaction. Its return to the market comes after years of public interest in the piece.What makes the original Thriller jacket so valuableThe red-and-black leather jacket first appeared in Jackson’s 1983 Thriller music video, which helped redefine the music video as a form of cinematic entertainment. Designed by Deborah Nadoolman Landis, the garment featured exaggerated shoulders, a distinctive V-shaped silhouette, silver buckles and red silk lining.According to Julien’s Auctions, the jacket was created to give Jackson a strong visual presence on screen. Its striking shape complemented the choreography, making the outfit as memorable as the music and dance sequences themselves.The jacket also helped spark a fashion trend during the 1980s. Julien’s Auctions notes that replicas became popular among young fans, with both authorised and unauthorised versions appearing on the market. The look remained closely associated with Jackson throughout his career, inspiring variations created for his later live performances.The original jacket has an important auction history of its own. It sold for approximately $1.8 million in 2011, setting a record for a jacket sold at auction. Africanews reported that Julien’s Auctions now believes the piece could sell for more than $10 million. But the auction house has not published a formal estimate for the jacket in its latest announcement.The jacket carries a personal connection to Jackson’s costume designersBeyond its place in music history, the jacket has a personal story connected to Jackson’s longtime costume designers, Michael Bush and Dennis Tompkins.Jackson brought the original garment to the designers and asked them to create a pattern that would allow similar jackets to be made for future performances. He had apparently expected the process might require them to damage the original, but they managed to reproduce its design without destroying it.Pleased with their work, Jackson gave them the jacket as a gesture of appreciation. The inside lining bears a personal inscription addressed to Bush and Dennis, while the sleeve carries another message signed by the singer.International exhibitions are bringing the memorabilia to fansBefore the December auction, selected items from the collection are travelling to several locations for public previews. Julien’s Auctions unveiled the highlights in Los Angeles on 7 October before taking a selection to Japan.According to MJVibe, the exhibition at Hankyu Umeda Main Store in Osaka ran from 9 to 12 October 2026. Around 50 selected objects associated with Jackson and Princess Diana were displayed, offering visitors a closer look at memorabilia scheduled for upcoming sales.The original Thriller jacket and the moonwalk glove were among the principal attractions. Other items included Jackson’s Thriller music video loafers and a distinctive illuminated jacket from his 1988 Bad Tour.MJVibe reported that the Bad Tour jacket, featuring built-in lights, illuminated again for the first time in 38 years. Costume designer Michael Bush attended the exhibition to discuss the garment and its history.Further previews are planned for Los Angeles, New York, Bahrain and Abu Dhabi. The final exhibition will take place ahead of the December auctions at the Rosewood Abu Dhabi, giving international visitors an opportunity to see the objects before bidding begins.You use AI every day. articles.title: In Norway, painting the bottom 10 metres of wind turbines black was linked to 48% fewer willow ptarmigan carcasses; evidence birds may hit the tower, not blades
articles.summary: A study at Smøla wind-power plant reveals that painting the lower 10 metres of wind turbine towers black significantly reduces willow ptarmigan carcasses, suggesting that the tower itself poses a major collision risk. Researchers urge further testing across different sites.
articles.body: A study that was published in Ecology and Evolution in April 2020 examined turbines at the Smøla wind-power plant, where researchers suspected that some birds were striking the tower itself rather than the moving blades. They compared painted turbines with nearby unpainted controls and found fewer recorded ptarmigan carcasses per search at the towers that had been treated. The findings suggest that the tower base can be a significant collision hazard for this ground-dwelling bird, although the researchers did not conclude that all collisions occurred with the tower.The tower may be the overlooked hazardWind turbine bird deaths are often associated with rotating blades, but at Smøla, researchers had found willow ptarmigan (Lagopus lagopus) carcasses close to turbine bases, sometimes with injuries that are consistent with a collision against a hard surface. The study cited earlier observations which showed that 138 of 142 recorded flights by flushed willow ptarmigan were below 15 metres, and that height overlaps with the lower section of a turbine tower.Some carcasses were found only a few metres from the tower base, and while the evidence did not rule out blade strikes, it did raise the possibility that the tower itself accounted for a major share of ptarmigan deaths at the site. Researchers painted the lower 10 metres of selected turbine towers black to test a possible remedy, and the darker section was intended to increase contrast between the tower and its surroundings, which made the structure easier for low-flying birds to see and avoid.Researchers compared painted and unpainted turbinesThe experiment took place at the Smøla wind-power plant, which is an island site off Norway’s central coast, where researchers painted four turbine bases in August 2014 and six more in July 2015, while ten neighbouring turbines remained unpainted and served as controls. The research team compared carcass-search records before and after painting, and accounted for the number of searches carried out. Across the study period, the researchers recorded 474 bird carcasses at the wind farm, including 194 willow ptarmigan.The analysis found a 48.2% reduction in the annual number of recorded ptarmigan carcasses per search at painted turbines relative to unpainted controls, and also found that ptarmigan carcasses were located farther from painted towers after treatment. However, the authors reported variation between years, and the result does not establish that painting would produce the same reduction at every wind farm.Blade painting may address a different riskA second study was published in Ecology and Evolution in July 2020, which found that the annual number of recorded bird carcasses per turbine fell by more than 70% at turbines with a painted blade compared with nearby unpainted controls. That experiment focused on rotor-blade visibility, while the ptarmigan study examined the lower tower, and the findings point to two different potential collision hazards, rather than a single explanation for bird deaths at wind farms.A practical measure that needs wider testingWind turbines can affect birds through collisions, habitat changes and other disturbances, and the US Fish and Wildlife Service says that the risk depends on factors including turbine location, design and the movement patterns of birds in the area. The Smøla findings give researchers a potential way to address tower collisions without changing how a turbine generates electricity, but the study authors recommended further testing to establish whether the effect applies to other locations and species. The 48% reduction is evidence from one Norwegian wind farm and one bird species for now, and does not establish that painting turbine bases black will reduce overall bird mortality by the same amount everywhere.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, a University of Waterloo team gave a small vertical-axis turbine blades that changed pitch; outdoor tests raised its power output by 22%
articles.summary: A groundbreaking small vertical-axis wind turbine developed by University of Waterloo researchers demonstrates a remarkable 22% increase in power output by enabling blades to change pitch during operation, improving efficiency and performance in fluctuating wind conditions.
articles.body: Researchers at the University of Waterloo built a small vertical-axis wind turbine that produced around 22% more power when its blades could change their angle during operation, as compared to a configuration in which the blades stayed fixed. The result came from outdoor tests that were described in a 2019 engineering thesis by Abdalrahman Gebreel, with the prototype making use of an automated control system to adjust blade pitch in response to wind conditions that were constantly changing. The research combined computer modelling with physical testing, but it is important to understand that the reported gain applies to the experimental turbine, not wind turbines generally.The blades changed angle as the wind shiftedVertical-axis wind turbines are different from the familiar three-bladed machines that rotate around a horizontal axis, since their rotor spins around a vertical shaft, and their blades move through the wind from different directions during each rotation. The arrangement can suit some small-scale applications, but extracting energy from changing airflow in an efficient manner is still a design challenge. Gebreel’s research examined an H-type Darrieus turbine, which is a design with straight vertical blades, which he used to investigate whether he could improve aerodynamic performance by controlling the angle of those blades and help the turbine start rotating.The research began with computational fluid dynamics simulations, with the models examining airflow around the blades at different pitch angles and operating conditions, and the results helped researchers identify suitable angles and develop a control system for the physical prototype. The University of Waterloo’s Computational Fluid Dynamics and Turbulence Modeling Laboratory describes the system as an intelligent vertical-axis wind turbine design, and its research page explains that the team used a combination of a conventional proportional-integral-derivative controller and a machine-learning method called a multilayer perceptron artificial neural network. The system used wind-speed measurements to determine how the blades should move.A controller adjusted each bladeThe prototype used a small electric motor and a four-bar linkage mechanism to adjust the pitch of each blade individually while an anemometer measured wind speed, and the controller used that information to command the blade adjustments. Pitch control is important because a blade’s angle has an effect on how air flows around its surface and how much useful force it generates. A fixed blade must operate through changing aerodynamic conditions as the rotor turns, while an adjustable blade can change its orientation to improve performance under different conditions.The researchers tested the prototype outdoors under different wind conditions and compared fixed-pitch and variable-pitch configurations. The thesis reports that the variable-pitch approach improved power output by approximately 22%, and also examined the turbine’s ability to start rotating, which is another challenge for some vertical-axis designs. The result was an experimental performance gain and not evidence that every small wind turbine would generate 22% more electricity with the same mechanism. The performance of a commercial installation would depend on factors such as turbine size, wind conditions, control-system reliability, and the energy that was consumed by the adjustment mechanism.What the design still needs to establishThe US Department of Energy explains that vertical-axis turbines are a separate category from the horizontal-axis machines that are more common. Darrieus designs use aerodynamic lift to turn their blades, while Savonius turbines rely primarily on drag, with the department also stating that vertical-axis turbines have not reached the same level of use in utility-scale wind generation as compared to horizontal-axis systems. Automated pitch control is one way by which researchers are trying to improve the performance of smaller vertical-axis machines, with the Waterloo prototype showing that blade movement could be controlled during outdoor operation and that the variable-pitch configuration could produce more power in the reported tests. The next question is how reliably the system performs over longer periods and across a wider range of wind speeds, and while the 22% figure offers a benchmark for the prototype, additional testing would be needed to establish how the design performs in practical installations.You use AI every day.
